prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling time and frequency measurement at unprecedented precision

statement.case_for: After reading all eight openings I keep B007 first, and the convergence is informative because it comes from members with different fields: three first places, six top-three rankings, and Katori and Ye proposed identically by all seven who ranked it. The case rests on what the Statutes and our own practice ask for. It is an original experimental invention, a new instrument, not a lifetime achievement or a later refinement. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice (2001-2003) removed the light-shift problem that had stopped neutral-atom trapping from being used for precision spectroscopy, and the first lattice clock demonstrations followed from his group. Ye's group then took the strontium system to the 1e-18 level and showed what the many-body lattice could do. The result is experimentally verified in the strongest sense: several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST, NPL) build such clocks and their comparisons agree, including over fibre links. It also opens a door, which matters to me: millimetre-scale relativistic redshift measurements, searches for variation of constants and for dark matter, and the planned redefinition of the second. The two-name credit is clean, and the first-demonstration question is one I can check against the record rather than leave to memory.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to what the committee has already honoured: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and precision spectroscopy and the 2012 prize covered quantum control of single ions, so some will read optical lattice clocks as a continuation. A second concern is attribution. Lattice clocks emerged alongside ion clocks, and the credit for the first lattice demonstration versus the push to record accuracy is claimed in different ways by Katori's and Ye's groups, with other contributors (for example Lemonde and Pal'chikov on magic-wavelength ideas) outside the supplied credit. Third, the SI redefinition has not yet happened, so a cautious member could argue the impact is still prospective. I think these are real but do not outweigh the verified, reproduced result and the clear originality of the magic-wavelength concept.

responses.point: Ranks B007 first as a textbook case of a measurement technique that moved the precision frontier by orders of magnitude, and flags that the prior comb and ion-clock prizes may be seen as covering part of the territory, and that the committee might prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with the measurement argument and I share the worry about overlap, but I would not wait for the redefinition. The prize is for the original discovery or invention, not for the institutional adoption that follows it, and the science is already confirmed by independent comparisons. The overlap concern is better answered on attribution grounds: the comb and ion-control prizes honoured different inventions, and the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate original idea with its own experimental demonstration. Where I differ from Stefan is on the priority question he says he is relying on memory for. We should check the 2001-2003 proposal and the first lattice-clock papers before the citation is fixed, since I want to be absolutely sure Katori's role is described correctly.

responses.point: Ranks B012 (IceCube) first as an instrument-driven discovery opening a new window on the universe, keeping the prize to Halzen and Karle, but concedes that individual credit is hard in a collaboration of a thousand people, with AMANDA and Baikal precursors and uncertain source-identification significance.
responses.response: I respect the instrument argument; a cubic-kilometre detector in ice is a real achievement and I understand why it attracts you. My serious reservation is exactly the one Mark himself raises: our rule is that we must find the people who did the original work, and for IceCube the original discovery is a collaboration result, with the 2013 discovery analysis, AMANDA and DUMAND as precursors, and source evidence (NGC 1068 near 4 sigma) that is still building. I would be uncomfortable naming Halzen and Karle until I know whose idea and whose analysis the diffuse-flux discovery really was. Compared with that, the attribution in B007 is simple and independently verifiable. I would keep B012 as my second alternative and revisit it in a later round if the authorship question can be settled.

responses.point: Puts B012 first and B005 second, calling twisted bilayer graphene a natural theory-plus-experiment story whose discovery is solid even though the pairing mechanism is debated, and noting that Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Yankowitz and Kim groups also played significant roles.
responses.response: I ranked B005 third myself and agree with Ulf that the discovery is original and demonstrably fertile, which is why it is my first alternative. But I weigh the open mechanism and sample dependence more heavily than he does: twist-angle disorder still makes the superconducting results device-dependent, and Yuan Cao, who did the 2018 experiments, is not among the credited names. A prize for an experimental discovery whose first author is left out would not satisfy my test of crediting those who did the original work. I would be ready to support B005 in a few years, or now if colleagues in condensed matter can show the credit allocation is defensible, but I do not see it as ahead of the lattice clock today.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED (B044) first as the architecture behind superconducting quantum processors, while acknowledging that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits may make the field look too recently honoured and that Blais's role as lead author of the theory proposal is a real allocation question.
responses.response: Göran is open about his closeness to this community, and I take his point that circuit QED opened a new strong-coupling regime on a chip. My concern is the one he raises, plus a second: the 2025 prize has just touched the same platform, and the credit among four names (Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf, Wallraff) cannot be settled within three. Importance to quantum computing is also not the same thing as the original discovery, which is the criterion I keep returning to. I would not rank it ahead of B007, but I welcome a fuller account from him of which step, the 2004 theory or the experiment, he considers decisive.

uncertainties: Exact priority between Katori's lattice demonstrations and the JILA/Ye work, and whether other proponents of the magic-wavelength concept need to be considered, is not verified from the files and must be checked against the record.
Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether the IceCube credit (B012) can be reduced to named individuals defensibly; I currently lack the information to judge this.
statement.conflict_note: No personal conflict apparent. One institutional connection to note: I hold a Fellowship at the University of Tokyo and have long-running exchanges with Tokyo, Kyushu and Tohoku communities, and Katori is, as far as I recall, associated with the University of Tokyo and RIKEN; the provided profile shows no collaboration or co-authorship with any shortlisted candidate. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson champions B044, which is not my preferred option, so I see no recusal issue there either.
